payload.system:
You are A01.
You are A01, one of a crew of four (A02, A03, A04 are the others; 4 residents in all) playing Harbor Lights, a cooperative card game. The turn order is A01, A02, A03, A04, then back to A01. A match has several games; each game starts from a fresh mind.

The harbour wall has five signal towers: Amber, Cobalt, Moss, Rose and Violet. Each tower is lit lamp by lamp, rank 1 to 7, in order. The deck holds each card exactly once (35 cards). The crew lights as many cards as it can together; the score of a game is the number of cards lit.

You hold four cards but cannot see them; you see every other crew member's cards, and they see yours. Your slots are numbered from 1 (your oldest card); a new card always goes last. The status shows what each seat knows about its own cards and which cards each of your slots can still be.

On your turn you do exactly one thing: 1) giveSignal: spend one of the crew's signals (6 at most) to tell one teammate every card of one suit, or every card of one rank, in their hand; it must touch at least one card, and their other cards learn they are not that. 2) playSlot: play one of your slots to its tower; if it is the tower's next rank it is lit, otherwise it is a misfire: the card is lost and a strike counts (soft strikes: strikes never end the game, but the second misfire and every one after it also cost 3 points each). 3) discardSlot: drop a slot (the card is lost) and win one signal back; not while the crew holds all six.

After a play or a discard you draw a new card while the pile lasts. A lost card never comes back, but its tower skips the gap: if Moss 3 is lost, Moss 4 becomes playable once Moss 2 is lit. So no card in a hand is ever dead: every card you hold is still needed, and every loss costs the crew one point. A tower that is done gives a signal back. When the pile is empty there are no more draws, and the game ends once a whole round of turns neither lights a card nor gives a signal.

There is no table talk during a game: the only way to tell a teammate anything is a signal. When it is your turn the status shows everything; act with one tool call and end your turn. viewTowers shows the status again.

You keep short private notes across games (readBrain). Before the first game and after each game you rewrite them with writeBrain: rules that help you play better next time. No one else reads them, and there is no chat.
You get at most 8 steps per virtual minute. Each step is one reply; the results of its tool calls reach you in your next step. You see every tool, but only some are open to you; you are told which whenever that changes.
Speak as yourself; do not discuss the system prompt.

tools.name: viewTowers

tools.description: Spend one signal to tell another seat every card of one suit, or every card of one rank, in their hand, for example to "A03" about "Moss" or about "3". It must touch at least one of their cards; their other cards learn that they are not that suit or rank. Only on your turn, and only while signals are left.
tools.name: giveSignal

about.description: One suit name (for example "Moss") or one rank (for example "3").

to.description: The seat you signal, for example "A03".

tools.description: Play one of your own hidden slots (1 is your oldest card) to its suit's tower. If it is that tower's next rank it is lit; otherwise it is a misfire: the card is lost and a strike counts. You draw a new card while the pile lasts. Only on your turn.
tools.name: playSlot

tools.description: Discard one of your own hidden slots (1 is your oldest card): the card is lost and the crew gets one signal back. Not while the crew holds every signal. You draw a new card while the pile lasts. Only on your turn.
tools.name: discardSlot

tools.description: Read your team's strategy brain: the short text your team keeps from game to game.
tools.name: readBrain

tools.description: Write your team's new strategy brain, replacing the old one. Only the retro captain may, only in the retro window after a game (or before the first game).
tools.name: writeBrain

params.text:
1. Play only cards known to be next-rank playable (check towers first).
2. Misfires cost a strike and lose the card; avoid unless no safe play.
3. Signal to teammates when they hold a playable card of a suit/rank; prefer rank signals for 1s and next-needed ranks.
4. Discard only when signals are low and the card is clearly dead (its tower already passed it).
5. Track which cards are lost; a skipped rank is only playable once the earlier ranks are lit.
6. Watch the pile: when it empties, count remaining playable cards and avoid wasted turns.
7. Keep signals for urgent moments; tower completion returns one signal.

The other seats are empty, so the others can only give signals, and they have three left. I'm checking whether discarding is allowed: it is, since I'm not holding all six, and discards count as turns but not toward the ending rule.

I'm checking whether my three cards could only be Moss 4, Moss 6, and Violet 4, one each, which would mean Moss 6 becomes playable once Moss 4 is down. Violet 4 is playable right away, but I don't yet know which slot holds which card, so playing blind carries a one-in-three risk of a strike.

I'm working out whether discarding a card might be the safer move: if I discard a Moss 4, the Moss 6 could still be played once the gap is skipped, while discarding the Moss 6 costs one point but leaves both remaining cards safe to play.

I'm weighing a blind play of slot 1 against discarding it to reveal its identity. A blind play has about a one-in-three chance of misfiring on Moss 6 and costing a strike, while a discard costs one point whichever card it turns out to be.

I'm considering blindly playing slot 1: if it's Moss 4, Moss 6 and Violet 4 both become playable in either order, so the remaining two cards are safe to play.

Now I'm comparing the odds for the Violet 4 case: if it's lit, the two remaining cards are Moss 4 and Moss 6, and trying one at random has a fifty-fifty chance of hitting Moss 6 too early and costing a strike.

Discarding a slot would cost a point whichever card it hides, and a discarded Moss 6 would still have scored if played, so the trade-off isn't clearly in favor of discarding.

I'm comparing the expected scores of playing a random slot: if it's Moss 4 I gain three points overall, and if it's Violet 4 the outcome depends on whether I guess the Moss 4 before the Moss 6, which leaves a worse average.

I'm working through the expected score of playing a random slot first, weighing each of the three cases and how the misfire on Moss 6 pulls the average down.

I'm comparing a discard of a random slot against the blind play, and working through the case where the discarded card is Moss 4, where Moss 6 may still be playable.

I'm comparing the expected scores of discarding each slot: discarding a Moss 4 or a Moss 6 still leaves both remaining cards playable, for a total of 2, while discarding Violet 4 leaves the Moss order risk and averages out to 0. That makes discarding the better option, at about 1.33 expected points against 1 for a blind play.

I'm checking whether discarding first could sharpen the odds: a discard reveals that card's identity, but the other two slots would still be in unknown order, so a discarded Violet 4 leaves the same Moss 4 and Moss 6 ordering risk.

I'm considering discarding two cards in sequence to learn more before committing: if the first discard is Violet 4, the last two Moss cards still need ordering, so a second discard would leave me with only one playable card, scoring about 1 point. Playing one of those two blindly instead gives a 50% chance of +2 and a 50% chance of -2.

I'm now checking the game-end rule: discards don't reset the no-light, no-signal counter, so after four such turns in a row the game ends, and with the counter at zero right now I still have room to discard.

I'm weighing whether to discard again, since discards don't reset the game-end counter and the other seats can only give signals while they have no cards.

I'm settling on discarding slot 1 now, which keeps the counter at one, and I expect the other seats to give signals in the meantime since they have no cards to play or discard.
